The procedure of trust

Market operation

The Market Operation pillar describes the operational rules of each sub-market: remuneration, the remunerated product attribute, clearing type, procurement frequency and the properties of accepted bids.

Return to feedback section

Source-grounded tutorial

How to think about this pillar

This pillar is where market design becomes a repeatable transaction process. It does not describe prequalification, baselining or settlement as separate pillar features; rather, the TMF pillar focuses on how bids are paid, what is paid, how the market is cleared, how often it runs and what bid forms are accepted. OneNet D11.2 explicitly adds Bid properties to the earlier framework.

OneNet D11.2 — updated TMF, Chapter 5.1Troncia et al. (2023) — TMF and OneNet lessons

Market-design intelligence

Read the pillar as a design procedure

Use this pillar to translate the market concept into rules that participants can act on and market operators can implement consistently.

1. Define the remuneration scheme

The TMF distinguishes no remuneration, negotiated price, pay-as-bid, uniform pay-as-clear, non-uniform pay-as-clear/nodal pricing, and cost-based remuneration. The 2023 paper explains how these schemes differ in the price received by successful providers.

2. Specify what product attribute is remunerated

The framework records whether payment is for availability, activation, or both, and whether the remunerated quantity concerns active, reactive or apparent power. This is important when capacity is reserved ahead of delivery and activation is settled later.

3. Choose continuous or discrete clearing

In a continuous market, participants can trade while the market is open. In a discrete market, clearing takes place in scheduled batches at defined intervals. The choice must match the timing and operational purpose of the service.

4. Define procurement frequency separately from market timing

Procurement frequency records how often the sub-market runs. It is not the same as GOT/GCT: two markets can both run daily yet close at different times before delivery.

5. Define the admissible bid format

D11.2 adds Bid properties to capture minimum bid size and bid structure. These features matter for participation barriers and compatibility with other markets, including bid-forwarding possibilities.

6. Review the operational trade-offs highlighted by OneNet

The OneNet analysis does not identify one universally superior remuneration, procurement timing or clearing type. Availability procurement can increase confidence and extend the procurement window, while near-delivery procurement may benefit from better system information. The appropriate choice remains service- and context-specific.

Evidence from OneNet

Why these choices matter in real market design

The OneNet assessment treats operation choices as case-specific. Remuneration, availability/activation procurement, timing and clearing mode interact with liquidity, competition, information quality and participation barriers.

Pricing rules cannot be assessed independently of market conditions

OneNet demonstrators use both pay-as-bid and pay-as-clear. The assessment discusses competition, product homogeneity and locational differentiation as factors that affect the suitability of a pricing rule.

Source: OneNet D11.2, §6 pricing-scheme assessment

Availability and activation solve different timing needs

Reserving availability in advance can increase SO confidence that flexibility will be present, while procuring closer to delivery benefits from better information. The suitable arrangement is service- and context-dependent.

Source: Troncia et al. (2023), §4.4

Procurement frequency is not gate timing

Markets may run at the same frequency while having different closure times. Keeping this distinction explicit is necessary when assessing coordination and bid-forwarding compatibility.

Source: Troncia et al. (2023), §2.4

Bid properties affect participation and interoperability

D11.2 identifies minimum bid size and bid structure as operational features. Its bid-forwarding analysis shows that differences in minimum size or product structure can require aggregation or other processing before bids can move between markets.

Source: OneNet D11.2, §5.1.4 and §5.2

Standard terminology repository

Definitions used by the TMF

These definitions focus on the operational features that the TMF assigns to each individual sub-market. Market phases such as prequalification, activation, measurement and settlement are treated elsewhere in D11.2 and should not be confused with the pillar’s feature set.

Remuneration scheme

The rule used to determine payment for successful market participation. TMF options include no remuneration, negotiated price, pay-as-bid, uniform pay-as-clear, non-uniform pay-as-clear and cost-based remuneration.

Source: Troncia et al. (2023), §2.4 / OneNet D11.2 Fig. 5.5

Negotiated price

A price agreed through bilateral negotiation between the relevant parties.

Source: Troncia et al. (2023), §2.4

Pay-as-bid

A discriminatory-price auction in which each successful seller is paid the price requested in its accepted bid.

Source: Troncia et al. (2023), §2.4

Uniform pay-as-clear

A uniform-price auction in which successful sellers receive the same per-unit clearing price for the homogeneous good or service.

Source: Troncia et al. (2023), §2.4

Non-uniform pay-as-clear / nodal pricing

A clearing approach with different prices at different grid nodes, reflecting locational value including congestion and delivery effects.

Source: Troncia et al. (2023), §2.4

Cost-based remuneration

Payment based on a price or price curve set by the system operator for buying the service, potentially with an agreed quantity.

Source: Troncia et al. (2023), §2.4

Remunerated product attribute

The product component for which payment is made: availability, activation, or both; D11.2 also distinguishes active, reactive and apparent power.

Source: Troncia et al. (2023), §2.4 / OneNet D11.2 Fig. 5.5

Continuous clearing

A market arrangement in which participants can buy or sell while the market is open.

Source: Troncia et al. (2023), §2.4

Discrete clearing

A recurring scheduled batch-clearing arrangement in which the market is cleared at discrete intervals.

Source: Troncia et al. (2023), §2.4

Procurement frequency

How often the sub-market is run. This is distinct from the gate timing/GCT of the individual market session.

Source: Troncia et al. (2023), §2.4

Bid properties

An additional D11.2 market-operation feature describing the nature of accepted bids through minimum bid size and bid structure.

Source: OneNet D11.2, §5.1.4

Minimum bid size

The minimum volume of capacity or energy that a bid must contain in the market.

Source: OneNet D11.2, Table 2.1

Bid structure

The level of complexity permitted in a bid; the TMF distinguishes simple and complex structures at high level.

Source: OneNet D11.2, Table 2.1 / Fig. 5.5

Apply the pillar

Expert mapping checklist

Use these checks when you map an existing market or test whether the pillar can guide a new design.

  • Can a reviewer identify exactly how accepted providers are paid?
  • Is it explicit whether availability, activation or both are remunerated and for which power quantity?
  • Is the market continuous or discrete, and how often is it run?
  • Are minimum bid size and bid structure explicit enough to judge participation barriers and cross-market compatibility?
  • Are operational choices being confused with separate processes such as prequalification or settlement, which the TMF treats elsewhere?
